grounding.derivation: The prefix test independently specifies that earlier released statuses retain their own ctx/from. Peer.ReadIndex accepts the supplied SystemCtx as request identity, and the public interface promises an outcome for the returned request. The actual requester consumes readiness by exact SystemCtx; no index-only association or prefix-completion API exists there. Consequently remote publication of a released status must carry that status identity to its requester. This is a local correlation duty, not an inference that every admitted read must succeed before its timeout. The release handler is implementation evidence and the suspected deviation, not normative authority by itself.
grounding.applicability: Only confirmed prefix members in the same leader readIndex lifetime are covered. Transport loss before confirmation does not excuse misidentification after the implementation elects to release a request.

materials.text:
managing its CPU, storage and network resources. Each NodeHost can manage Raft
nodes from many different Raft groups known as Raft clusters. Each Raft cluster
is identified by its ClusterID and it usually consists of multiple nodes, each
identified its NodeID value. Nodes from the same Raft cluster can be considered
as replicas of the same data, they are suppose to be distributed on different
NodeHost instances across the network, this brings fault tolerance to machine
and network failures as application data stored in the Raft cluster will be
available as long as the majority of its managing NodeHost instances (i.e. its
underlying hosts) are available.

User applications can leverage the power of the Raft protocol implemented in
dragonboat by implementing the IStateMachine or IOnDiskStateMachine component,
as defined in github.com/lni/dragonboat/v3/statemachine. Known as user state
machines, each IStateMachine and IOnDiskStateMachine instance is in charge of
updating, querying and snapshotting application data with minimum exposure to
the complexity of the Raft protocol implementation.

User applications can use NodeHost's APIs to update the state of their
IStateMachine or IOnDiskStateMachine instances, this is called making proposals.
Once accepted by the majority nodes of a Raft cluster, the proposal is
considered as committed and it will be applied on all member nodes of the Raft
cluster. Applications can also make linearizable reads to query the state of the
IStateMachine or IOnDiskStateMachine instances. Dragonboat employs the ReadIndex
protocol invented by Diego Ongaro for fast linearizable reads.

Dragonboat guarantees the linearizability of your I/O when interacting with the
IStateMachine or IOnDiskStateMachine instances. In plain English, writes (via
making proposal) to your Raft cluster appears to be instantaneous, once a write
is completed, all later reads (linearizable read using the ReadIndex protocol
as implemented and provided in dragonboat) should return the value of that write
or a later write. Once a value is returned by a linearizable read, all later
reads should return the same value or the result of a later write.

To strictly provide such guarantee, we need to implement the at-most-once
semantic required by linearizability. For a client, when it retries the proposal
that failed to complete before its deadline during the previous attempt, it has
the risk to have the same proposal committed and applied twice into the user
state machine. Dragonboat prevents this by implementing the client session
concept described in Diego Ongaro's PhD thesis.

Arbitrary number of Raft clusters can be launched across the network
simultaneously to aggregate distributed processing and storage capacities. Users
can also make membership change requests to add or remove nodes from any
interested Raft cluster.

NodeHost APIs for making the above mentioned requests can be loosely classified
into two categories, synchronous and asynchronous APIs. Synchronous APIs will
not return until the completion of the requested operation. Their method names
all start with Sync*. The asynchronous counterparts of such synchronous APIs,
on the other hand, usually return immediately. This allows users to concurrently
initiate multiple such asynchronous operations to save the total amount of time
required to complete all of them.

Dragonboat is a feature complete Multi-Group Raft implementation - snapshotting,
membership change, leadership transfer, non-voting members and disk based state
machine are all provided.

Dragonboat is also extensively optimized. The Raft protocol implementation is
fully pipelined, meaning proposals can start before the completion of previous

func lw(r *raft, f func(m pb.Message, rp *remote)) handlerFunc {
	w := func(nm pb.Message) {
		if npr, ok := r.remotes[nm.From]; ok {
			f(nm, npr)
		} else if nob, ok := r.observers[nm.From]; ok {
			f(nm, nob)
		} else if wob, ok := r.witnesses[nm.From]; ok {
			f(nm, wob)
		} else {
			plog.Warningf("%s no remote for %s", r.describe(), NodeID(nm.From))
			return
		}
	}
	return w
}

func defaultHandle(r *raft, m pb.Message) {
	f := r.handlers[r.state][m.Type]
	if f != nil {
		f(m)
	}
}

func (r *raft) initializeHandlerMap() {
	// candidate
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.Heartbeat] = r.handleCandidateHeartbeat
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.Propose] = r.handleCandidatePropose
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.ReadIndex] = r.handleCandidateReadIndex
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.Replicate] = r.handleCandidateReplicate
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.InstallSnapshot] = r.handleCandidateInstallSnapshot
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.RequestVoteResp] = r.handleCandidateRequestVoteResp
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.Election] = r.handleNodeElection
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.RequestVote] = r.handleNodeRequestVote
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.ConfigChangeEvent] = r.handleNodeConfigChange
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.LocalTick] = r.handleLocalTick
	r.handlers[candidate][pb.SnapshotReceived] = r.handleRestoreRemote
	// follower
	r.handlers[follower][pb.Propose] = r.handleFollowerPropose
	r.handlers[follower][pb.Replicate] = r.handleFollowerReplicate
	r.handlers[follower][pb.Heartbeat] = r.handleFollowerHeartbeat
	r.handlers[follower][pb.ReadIndex] = r.handleFollowerReadIndex
	r.handlers[follower][pb.LeaderTransfer] = r.handleFollowerLeaderTransfer
	r.handlers[follower][pb.ReadIndexResp] = r.handleFollowerReadIndexResp
	r.handlers[follower][pb.InstallSnapshot] = r.handleFollowerInstallSnapshot
	r.handlers[follower][pb.Election] = r.handleNodeElection
	r.handlers[follower][pb.RequestVote] = r.handleNodeRequestVote
	r.handlers[follower][pb.TimeoutNow] = r.handleFollowerTimeoutNow
	r.handlers[follower][pb.ConfigChangeEvent] = r.handleNodeConfigChange
	r.handlers[follower][pb.LocalTick] = r.handleLocalTick
	r.handlers[follower][pb.SnapshotReceived] = r.handleRestoreRemote
	// leader
	r.handlers[leader][pb.LeaderHeartbeat] = r.handleLeaderHeartbeat
	r.handlers[leader][pb.CheckQuorum] = r.handleLeaderCheckQuorum
	r.handlers[leader][pb.Propose] = r.handleLeaderPropose
	r.handlers[leader][pb.ReadIndex] = r.handleLeaderReadIndex
	r.handlers[leader][pb.ReplicateResp] = lw(r, r.handleLeaderReplicateResp)
	r.handlers[leader][pb.HeartbeatResp] = lw(r, r.handleLeaderHeartbeatResp)
	r.handlers[leader][pb.SnapshotStatus] = lw(r, r.handleLeaderSnapshotStatus)
	r.handlers[leader][pb.Unreachable] = lw(r, r.handleLeaderUnreachable)
	r.handlers[leader][pb.LeaderTransfer] = r.handleLeaderTransfer
	r.handlers[leader][pb.Election] = r.handleNodeElection
	r.handlers[leader][pb.RequestVote] = r.handleNodeRequestVote
	r.handlers[leader][pb.ConfigChangeEvent] = r.handleNodeConfigChange
	r.handlers[leader][pb.LocalTick] = r.handleLocalTick
	r.handlers[leader][pb.SnapshotReceived] = r.handleRestoreRemote
	r.handlers[leader][pb.RateLimit] = r.handleLeaderRateLimit
	// observer
	r.handlers[observer][pb.Heartbeat] = r.handleObserverHeartbeat
	r.handlers[observer][pb.Replicate] = r.handleObserverReplicate
	r.handlers[observer][pb.InstallSnapshot] = r.handleObserverSnapshot
	r.handlers[observer][pb.Propose] = r.handleObserverPropose
	r.handlers[observer][pb.ReadIndex] = r.handleObserverReadIndex
	r.handlers[observer][pb.ReadIndexResp] = r.handleObserverReadIndexResp
	r.handlers[observer][pb.ConfigChangeEvent] = r.handleNodeConfigChange
	r.handlers[observer][pb.LocalTick] = r.handleLocalTick
	r.handlers[observer][pb.SnapshotReceived] = r.handleRestoreRemote
	// witness
	r.handlers[witness][pb.Heartbeat] = r.handleWitnessHeartbeat
	r.handlers[witness][pb.Replicate] = r.handleWitnessReplicate
	r.handlers[witness][pb.InstallSnapshot] = r.handleWitnessSnapshot
	r.handlers[witness][pb.RequestVote] = r.handleNodeRequestVote
	r.handlers[witness][pb.ConfigChangeEvent] = r.handleNodeConfigChange
	r.handlers[witness][pb.LocalTick] = r.handleLocalTick
	r.handlers[witness][pb.SnapshotReceived] = r.handleRestoreRemote
}

feedback.answered: Initial A1 source trace: leader append assigns current term/index, updates its own match, and replication responses update remote match; tryCommit selects voting-member quorum match and asks the log to commit only in the current term. Followers validate the preceding log term, append, and bound advertised commit by the matched suffix. Initial A2 trace: elections reset term/votes/progress and gather votes after log freshness checks; higher-term dispatch changes role and lower-term messages are dropped. Reset discards pending read confirmations and initializes follower progress, while leader promotion appends a current-term no-op. Election is suppressed when committed work has not yet applied, with a comment explicitly tying this to membership/quorum safety. These traces do not yet establish persistence ordering or application/membership completion. Early sourced discrepancy: readIndex.confirm releases a prefix of pending requests and retains each request ctx/from, but handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation sends every remote response using the confirming message Hint/HintHigh, whereas local completion uses s.ctx. Followers copy the response context to ReadyToRead; pendingReadIndex.addReady selects a batch by exact SystemCtx. Thus a prefix request with a different context appears not to receive its own completion key. Timeout/GC exists and is contrary evidence against permanent resource retention; no execution or normative conclusion is claimed.
remaining: Complete the A1/A2 backbone through peer update, persistence/message ordering, application, membership changes, recovery and public completion contracts before registering a focused Candidate.

formation.explanation: Node batches proposals into Peer under raftMu. Leader stamps term/index, replicates to members and advances commitment from voting match order statistic only for its current term. Followers require preceding term match and protect the committed prefix, replying after engine persistence. Conflicts reduce next and retry; snapshots resynchronize missing history. Engine exposes committed entries to the RSM queue, whose application/session results and applied index drive client consumption. ReadIndex separately samples committed index, gathers heartbeat confirmation and releases pending prefixes to local readiness or remote responses.

context.explanation: Per-cluster term, role and applied membership define authority. Timers launch elections for eligible full members only after committed work is applied; votes require fresh log and no conflicting vote. Candidate quorum promotes and appends a current-term no-op. Higher terms demote/reset; lower terms are rejected. CheckQuorum may revoke leadership; transfer waits for target match and uses TimeoutNow, while proposals are dropped during transfer. Configuration application changes participant maps and local removal revokes leadership. Restart restores persisted term/vote/log but initializes transient follower context.

connection.explanation: Term dispatch precedes response consumption. Reset clears old votes, replication progress and pending ReadIndex support while retaining established log/commit; leader must form current-term commitment before multi-voter reads. Log freshness and committed-prefix protection constrain future leaders. Election waits for application so committed membership changes affect later quorums; RSM changes update Peer under raftMu. Old client work can be dropped or time out independently of preserved decisions. Read confirmation is transient; exact context and applied-index checks bridge its publication to requester completion, making remote prefix correlation a concrete unresolved consumption premise.

Reviewed fixed artifact e4465cc7b4964f2faf0e4099ccd60176, its stored plan and harness, and raw stdout/stderr for c611aead474d4b8fa96906fb00bd1771 against claim version 1. The duty is preservation of the original SystemCtx for each remote read released by prefix confirmation, supported by the explicit per-prefix ctx/from test expectation and exact-context consumer. It is not a successful-completion deadline. Launch constructs three configured full voters and bootstrap entries. The driver applies only committed bootstrap membership and the empty leader entry; it never changes term, role, pending reads or generated message contents. Tick-driven election actually reaches term 2 and current-term commit 4; setup assertions check all nodes committed/applied at 4 and known leader 1. Storage Append/SetState precedes message exposure; Update Commit and NotifyRaftLastApplied retain caller completion order for this synchronous non-crashing history. A globally FIFO queue is a permitted restriction of per-route ordering and does not serialize the two pending reads: both are observed pending before confirmation. The two first-context heartbeats are dropped at send admission, a failure explicitly permitted by Transport.send and not retried by NodeHost.sendMessage; later traffic is generated by real Peer handlers and delivered without reordering. The known-peer Peer.Handle checks and current-term checks remain active. No background owners, sleeps, shutdown, forged replies or hidden callbacks participate.

Raw events 18 and 19 admit distinct requester identities 2 and 3, with queued=true, two pending requests, current-term commit, sampled index 4 and original contexts (1001,101)/(2001,202). Both actual nonzero-context heartbeat replies originate from voters in term 2. The first suffices with leader self-support to release the prefix. Raw result 24 for requester 2 contains one response context (2001,202), released=true, leader_pending=0 and queue_empty=true; its actual follower ReadyToRead also contains (2001,202) at index 4. Result 25 for requester 3 contains its correct (2001,202), also released=true. Thus both antecedents are observed true, not vacuous. The raw wire records independently exhibit the wrong leader-to-2 response. The monitor correlates each admitted operation by scenario/requester, not the compared context, and checks exact serialized complete High/Low context lists. Both sides use the same Go struct encoder; the observed lists each have one element, so the decisive mismatch is content identity, not cardinality or order. A comparison on response count alone would miss it. The run has no parser gaps and both admissions have results. The sent slice is an immutable copied message history accumulated by the sole goroutine; ReadyToRead values are copied before Peer.Commit clears the producer queue. Absence from pending is valid release evidence in this suffix because no reset/removal path runs and source confirm is the deletion owner.

The implementation cause agrees with the measurement: confirm retains original s.ctx and s.from while releasing the prefix, but the remote send loop uses m.Hint/m.HintHigh for each s.from; the local branch correctly uses s.ctx. The exact-key client consumer cannot associate this wrong context with requester 2 original batch. That final NodeHost timeout consequence is source-supported risk, not an executed endpoint result. No correspondence issue was found for this complete local counterexample.

Explained alternatives and bounded contrary observations: The later request succeeds in the same run: requester 3 receives its own (2001,202), so the finding is not a blanket failure of remote ReadIndex. The source local-completion branch uses s.ctx correctly; no local-prefix violation is claimed. Requester timeout/GC remains available and prevents inferring permanent resource retention. The test process passed because it emitted measurements for the monitor; process success is not the property verdict.
items.report_title: 批量确认读取时，早期远端请求收到后一个请求的上下文
items.report_answer: 实测节点 2 的请求上下文为 (1001,101)，但领导者向它发送、且它接收的就绪结果均为后一个请求的 (2001,202)；两个请求都已从领导者待处理队列移除。该结果验证了稳定任期内前缀确认的远端请求身份丢失，不等同于已测得客户端超时或线性一致性破坏。
limitations: This is a Peer-level local correlation violation under fixed membership and a stable term, not an observed application-level stale read or cluster safety violation.
The singleton-list oracle is assessed for this one-request-per-requester, nonduplicating delivery history; this review does not assert a general prohibition on repeated identical network responses.
TestLogDB exercises successful storage API ordering but provides no filesystem/crash evidence.
No NodeHost pending batch, RequestState timeout, session endpoint or user state machine was executed; follower ReadyToRead is the immediate downstream observation.
